newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PARLIAMENT FOCUSES ON RAMPANT S.AFRICAN CRIME.
newsitem.headline: PARLIAMENT FOCUSES ON RAMPANT S.AFRICAN CRIME.

text.p: Tempers ran high in South Africa's parliament on Friday as the focus fell on the country's rampant crime rate.

Safety and Security Minister Sydney Mufamadi set the scene for the debate on his 1997/98 budget vote in the national assembly with a tally of the successes and failures of police over the last year in their bid to combat crime.

Aware from past experience that he was in for a torrid time from opposition MPs, Mufamadi appealed for a calm and rational debate that would "help all of us to define ways by which we can better contribute to the process of finding a solution to the problem which is causing untold suffering to our people."
His appeal largely fell on deaf ears.

For the next five hours, amid catcalls from the African National Congress ranks, opposition MPs blamed the crime rate on everything from mismanagement to affirmative action, the lifting of the death penalty and the invasion of illegal immigrants.

Many homed in on the recent fall-out between Mufamadi and his white commissioner, George Fivaz, about management issues which Mufamadi dismissed as an "unfortunate" boardroom squabble which "we cannot afford to repeat".
ANC MPs complained of continued racism by the police but said Mufamadi was doing the best he could with the racially divided police force he had inherited from the apartheid era.

Fivaz admitted that the police force, which employs 140,000 people and had a budget of 11.9 billion rand, had serious management problems and that he planned to recruit "the best expertise available in the country and abroad" to help out.
"I am committed to turning the (police) around," he said.
Mufamadi said South Africa continued to be "awash with a sea of firearms", even though police recorded an 11 percent increase in the number of illegal firearms seized to 18,059.

A large proportion of the crime problem was either organised or relied on some level of organisation, he said, while the justice system was being undermined by high levels of corruption and self-serving abuse.
